**Commentary on Surat al-Mujadila (Tafsir Surat al-Mujadila)**

It has twenty-two verses and is Medinan according to all scholars, except for a report from ʿAtaʾ that the first ten verses are Medinan and the rest Meccan. Al-Kalbi said that all of it was revealed in Medina except the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿There is no secret conference of three but He is their fourth﴾, which were revealed in Mecca.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Allah has heard the speech of the woman who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah. And Allah hears your mutual dialogue. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing.﴾ (58:1)

There are two issues.

The first is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah has heard the speech of the woman who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah.﴾ The woman who complained to Allah was Khawlah bint Thaʿlabah. It is also said she was the daughter of Hakim, and it is said her name was Jamilah. Khawlah is the most sound. Her husband was Aws ibn al-Samit, the brother of ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) passed by her during his caliphate while people were with him on a donkey. She stopped him for a long time and admonished him, saying: "O ʿUmar, you used to be called ʿUmayr, then you were called ʿUmar, then you were called Commander of the Faithful. So fear Allah, O ʿUmar. Whoever is certain of death fears missing [its preparation], and whoever is certain of the reckoning fears the punishment." He was standing and listening to her words. It was said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, do you stand for this old woman in this manner?" He said: "By Allah, if she had detained me from the beginning of the day until its end, I would not have left except for the obligatory prayer. Do you know who this old woman is? She is Khawlah bint Thaʿlabah. Allah heard her speech from above the seven heavens. Would the Lord of the worlds hear her speech and ʿUmar not hear it?"

ʿA'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "Blessed is He whose hearing encompasses all things. Indeed, I heard the speech of Khawlah bint Thaʿlabah, and some of it was hidden from me. She was complaining about her husband to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and saying: 'O Messenger of Allah! He has consumed my youth, and I have borne him many children. When my age advanced and my children ceased, he made me like his mother [through zihar]. O Allah, I complain to You!' She had not left before Jibril came down with this verse: ﴿Allah has heard the speech of the woman who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah.﴾" Ibn Majah recorded it in his Sunan.

What is in al-Bukhari on this from ʿA'ishah says: She said, "Praise be to Allah, whose hearing encompasses all voices. The woman who pleads (al-mujadilah) came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) complaining, while I was in a corner of the house and could not hear what she was saying. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Allah has heard the speech of the woman who pleads with you concerning her husband﴾."

Al-Mawardi said: She is Khawlah bint Thaʿlabah. It is also said: she is the daughter of Khuwaylid. This is not a contradiction, because one of them was her father and the other her grandfather, so she was attributed to each of them. Her husband was Aws ibn al-Samit, the brother of ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit.

Al-Tha'labi said, citing Ibn ʿAbbas: She is Khawlah bint Khuwaylid al-Khazrajiyyah. She was under Aws ibn al-Samit, the brother of ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit, and she was beautiful of body. Her husband saw her prostrating and looked at her buttocks, and her condition pleased him. When she finished, he wanted her, but she refused, so he became angry with her. Urwah [[Urwah is the narrator of the aforementioned hadith of ʿA'ishah.]] said: He was a man afflicted with lamam [[Al-lamam: a touch of madness that afflicts a person, meaning it overcomes him.]], and some of his lamam struck him, and he said to her: "You are to me like the back of my mother." Iilaʾ (oath of abstention) and zihar (the declaration of a wife to be like one's mother) were forms of divorce in the Jahiliyyah. She asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said to her: "You are forbidden to him." She said: "By Allah, he did not mention divorce." Then she said: "I complain to Allah of my poverty, my loneliness, my isolation, and the separation from my husband and my cousin, and I have borne him children." He said: "You are forbidden to him." She kept returning to him, and he kept returning to her, until this verse was revealed to him.

Al-Hasan narrated that she said: "O Messenger of Allah! Allah has abrogated the practices of the Jahiliyyah, and my husband has made zihar of me." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Nothing has been revealed to me about this." She said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are given revelation about everything, yet this has been hidden from you?!" He said: "It is what I told you." She said: "I complain to Allah, not to His Messenger."

So Allah revealed: ﴿Allah has heard the speech of the woman who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah﴾, to the end of the verse.

Al-Daraqutni narrated through Qatadah that Anas ibn Malik told him: "Aws ibn al-Samit made zihar of his wife Khuwaylah bint Thaʿlabah, and she complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). She said: 'He made zihar when my age advanced and my bones grew frail.' So Allah, the Exalted, revealed the verse of zihar. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Aws: 'Free a slave.' He said: 'I do not have the means for that.' He said: 'Then fast two consecutive months.' He said: 'If I do not eat three times in a day, my sight will weaken.' He said: 'Then feed sixty needy persons.' He said: 'I have nothing except that you assist me with some aid and gift.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) assisted him with fifteen sa's [[The gloss here is a measure of volume: a ṣāʿ is a traditional unit of dry measure.]] until Allah gathered [provision] for him. [And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.] [[The addition is from manuscripts ḥ, z, l, h.]]"

﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing.﴾ He said: So they used to think that He had something equal to it, which was for the sixty needy persons.

In al-Tirmidhi and Sunan Ibn Majah: Salamah ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi made zihar of his wife, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Free a slave." He said: "I struck the side of my neck with my hand and said: 'No, by the One who sent you with the truth, I do not own anything but her.' He said: 'Then fast two months.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, did I not suffer what I suffered only because of fasting?' He said: 'Then feed sixty needy persons.'" The hadith continues.

Ibn al-ʿArabi mentioned in his Ahkam: It is narrated that Khawlah bint Dulaij was made zihar of by her husband, so she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You have become forbidden to him." She said: "I complain to Allah of my need." [Then she returned and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You have become forbidden to him." She said: "To Allah I complain of my need of him." [[The addition is from Ibn al-ʿArabi's al-Ahkam.]]] ʿA'ishah was washing the right side of his head, then she moved to the other side, and revelation had come down to him. She was about to repeat [her words], but ʿA'ishah said: "Be quiet, for revelation has descended." When the Qur'an was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her husband: "Free a slave." He said: "I do not have one." He said: "Fast two consecutive months." He said: "If I do not eat three times a day, I fear my sight will become dim." He said: "Then feed sixty needy persons." He said: "Then help me." So he helped him with something.

Abu Jaʿfar al-Nahhas said: The scholars of tafsir hold that she was Khawlah and her husband was Aws ibn al-Samit. They differed about her lineage. Some said she was an Ansari woman and was the daughter of Thaʿlabah. Some said she was the daughter of Dulaij. It was said she was the daughter of Khuwaylid, and some said she was the daughter of al-Samit. Some said she was a slave girl belonging to ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy, and she is the one about whom Allah revealed: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution if they desire chastity﴾, because he used to compel her to fornication. It is also said she was the daughter of Hakim.

Al-Nahhas said: This is not contradictory. It is permissible for her to be attributed at one time to her father, at another to her mother, and at another to her grandfather. It is also permissible that she was a slave girl belonging to ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy, and so she was called Ansari by clientage, because he was counted among the Ansar, even though he was among the hypocrites.

The second issue: ﴿Qad sami'a Allah﴾ has been recited with idgham (assimilation of the two identical letters, the dal of qad into the sin of sami'a), and it has been recited with izhar (clear pronunciation without assimilation). The original meaning of al-sama' (hearing) is perceiving audible things. This is the view chosen by Shaykh Abu al-Hasan. Ibn Fawrak said: The correct view is that it is perceiving what is heard.

Al-Hakim Abu ʿAbdullah said regarding the meaning of al-Sami' (the Hearing): He is the One who perceives voices that created beings perceive with their ears, without having an ear. This returns to the fact that voices are not hidden from Him, even though He is not described by the physical sense placed in the ear. Just as the deaf person, lacking this faculty, is not capable of perceiving sound, so He is not limited in this way. Hearing and seeing are two attributes, like knowledge, power, life, and will. They are therefore among the attributes of the Essence; the Creator, glory be to Him and exalted, has never ceased to be described by them.

Shakā (شَكَى) and ishtakā (اشْتَكَى) have the same meaning. It was recited as تحاورك (tuhāwiruka), meaning she responds to you in speech, and تُجادِلُكَ (tujādiluka) means she questions you.

The passage contains twenty-three issues. The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those of you who liken their wives to their mothers' backs﴾ [[The original text was corrected to (yuzahiruna), which is the reading of Nafi' that the author uses in what follows.]]. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (yuzzaharuna), with a fatha on the ya', a shaddah on the za' and an alif. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read (yuzahiruna), without the alif, with shaddahs on the ha' and the za', and with a fatha on the ya'. Abu al-'Aliyah, 'Asim and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read (yuzahiruna), with a damma on the ya', a light za', an alif and a kasra on the ha'. This was discussed earlier in (al-Ahzab) [[See vol. 14, p. 118, where he mentioned nothing but referred the discussion to this surah.]]. In the reading of Ubayy it is (yatazahharuna), which has the same meaning as the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah. The back is mentioned as a metaphor for mounting, since a human being is not mounted on the belly; but the back is mentioned instead, because what is ridden among non-human animals is ridden on its back. Thus the back is used as a metaphor for riding. It is said: "He dismounted from his wife," meaning he divorced her, as if he had dismounted from a mount. The meaning of "You are to me like my mother's back" is: "You are forbidden to me; it is not lawful for me to ride you."

The second issue: The reality of zihar (the pre-Islamic formula of likening a wife to a woman forbidden to the husband, a form of divorce) is the likening of one back to another back. What makes the ruling apply is likening a lawful back to a forbidden back. For this reason the jurists agreed that whoever says to his wife, "You are to me like my mother's back," is a mudahir (one who commits zihar). Most of them held that if he says to her, "You are to me like my daughter's back," or "my sister's back," or anything of that kind from the women who are forbidden to him by kinship (dhawat al-mahram), he is a mudahir. This is the position of Malik, Abu Hanifah and others. There is a difference of opinion on this from al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him). It is narrated from him something like the view of Malik, because he has likened his wife to a permanently forbidden back, like the mother. Abu Thawr narrated from him that zihar occurs only with the mother alone. This is the position of Qatadah and al-Sha'bi. The first view is the position of al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, al-Awza'i and al-Thawri.

The third issue: The origin of zihar is that a man says to his wife, "You are to me like my mother's back." Allah mentioned the back as a metaphor for, and a covering of, the belly. If he says, "You are to me like my mother," without mentioning the back, or says, "You are to me like the likeness of my mother," then if he intended zihar, it is his intention that counts. If he intended divorce, then according to Malik he has divorced her irrevocably. If he had no intention of either divorce or zihar, he is a mudahir. The explicit wording of zihar does not turn into divorce by intention, just as the explicit wording of divorce and its well-known allusions do not turn into zihar. The allusive wording of zihar specifically turns into an irrevocable divorce by intention.

The fourth issue: The wordings of zihar are of two kinds: explicit (sarih) and allusive (kinayah). The explicit is: "You are to me like my mother's back," "You are with me," "You are from me," and "You are with me like my mother's back." Likewise: "You are to me like my mother's belly, or her head, or her private part, or the like." Similarly: "Your private part, or your head, or your back, or your belly, or your leg is to me like my mother's back," and he is a mudahir, just as with his saying, "Your hand, or your leg, or your head, or your private part is divorced," which causes divorce. Al-Shafi'i, in one of his two opinions, said that it is not zihar. This is weak from him, because he agreed with us that divorce can validly be attributed to the wife alone in a literal sense, against Abu Hanifah; so zihar may likewise be attributed to a part of her. Whenever he likens her to his mother or to one of his grandmothers, from his father's or his mother's side, it is zihar without disagreement. If he likens her to other women forbidden to him in no circumstances, such as a daughter, sister, paternal aunt or maternal aunt, he is a mudahir according to most jurists, and according to Imam al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him), in the sound view of his school, as we have mentioned. The allusive wording is that he says, "You are to me like my mother," or "like the likeness of my mother," and in this case his intention is considered. If he intended zihar, it is zihar; if he did not intend zihar, he is not a mudahir according to al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah. The position of Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) on this has already been mentioned. The evidence for it is that he applied the likening of his wife to his mother without qualification, so it was zihar, the origin being when he mentions the back. This is a strong argument, for the meaning of the wording is present in it, and the wording means its meaning. He was not bound by the ruling of the back because of the wording, but he was bound by its meaning, which is prohibition. This was said by Ibn al-'Arabi.

The fifth issue: If he likens the whole of his wife to a limb of his mother, he is a mudahir, against Abu Hanifah, who said that if he likens her to a limb that it is lawful for him to look at, he is not a mudahir. This is not correct, because looking at it with a view to enjoyment is not lawful for him, and it is in this that the likening occurs, and it is this that the mudahir intends. Al-Shafi'i said in one opinion that it is zihar only with the back alone. This is invalid, because every limb of hers is forbidden, so likening it is zihar like the back. And because the mudahir only intends to liken what is lawful to what is forbidden, so it is binding by the meaning.

The sixth issue: If he likens his wife to a non-related woman (ajnabiyyah), then if he mentions the back, it is zihar, by analogy with the first. If he does not mention the back, our scholars differed about it. Some of them said: it is zihar. Some said: it is divorce. Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: it is nothing. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is invalid, because he has likened a lawful woman to a forbidden one, so it is bound by its ruling, like the back. Names are by their meanings according to us, and according to them by their wordings; and this is a contradiction of their own principle. I say: The disagreement about zihar with a non-related woman is strong according to Malik. Among his companions, some do not consider zihar except with women forbidden by kinship alone, and do not consider zihar with other women. Some do not consider it anything. And some consider it, with a non-related woman, to be divorce. According to Malik, if he says, "Like the back of my son, or my slave, or like the back of Zayd, or like the back of a non-related woman," it is zihar, and it is not lawful for him to have intercourse with her during the time of his oath. It is also narrated from him that zihar with women other than those forbidden by kinship is nothing, as the Kufan and al-Shafi'i said. Al-Awza'i said: If he says to her, "You are to me like the back of so-and-so, a man," it is an oath, for which he must make expiation. And Allah knows best.

The seventh issue: If he says, "You are to me forbidden like my mother's back," it is zihar and not divorce, because his saying, "You are forbidden to me," admits of forbiddance by divorce, so she is divorced; and it admits of forbiddance by zihar. When he explicitly stated it, it became an explanation of one of the two possibilities, and the ruling follows from it.

The eighth issue: Zihar is binding in respect of every wife, whether consummated or unconsummated, in whatever condition she is, from a husband whose divorce is valid. Likewise, according to Malik, whoever may lawfully have intercourse with his slave-women, if he commits zihar with them, zihar binds him concerning them. Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: it is not binding. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: This is a very difficult issue for us, because Malik says: If he says to his slave-woman, "You are forbidden to me," it is not binding. How then is the explicit wording of forbiddance void in her case, while its allusive wording is valid? But the slave-woman enters into the generality of His saying: ﴿from their wives﴾, because He meant from their lawful women. The reason is that it is a wording connected with intercourse, without removing the contract; so it is valid for a slave-woman, its origin being the oath by Allah, exalted is He.

The ninth issue: Zihar is also binding before marriage, if he marries the woman with whom he committed zihar, according to Malik. It is not binding according to al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from their wives﴾, and she is not one of his wives. The origin of this issue has already passed in the surah (Bara'ah) at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 210.]], the verse.

The tenth issue: The dhimmi's (non-Muslim subject under Muslim rule) zihar is not binding. This was said by Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafi'i said: the zihar of a dhimmi is valid. Our evidence is His saying: ﴿from among you﴾, meaning from among the Muslims. This requires the exclusion of the dhimmi from the address. If it is said: this is an argument from the implication of the wording (dalil al-khitab). We say: It is an argument from derivation and meaning, for the marriages of the unbelievers are invalid and deserving of annulment, so no ruling of divorce or zihar attaches to them. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And call to witness two persons of justice﴾

(minkum) ﴿from among you﴾. When marriage contracts lack the conditions of validity, they are invalid, and there is no ẓihār (the pre-Islamic formula of likening one's wife to one's mother's back) in an invalid marriage under any circumstances.

**The eleventh issue:** His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿from among you﴾ requires that the ẓihār of a slave be valid, contrary to those who prohibited it. Al-Tha'labi reported this from Malik, because he is one of the Muslims, and the rulings of marriage apply to him, even if freeing a slave and feeding the poor are impossible for him, since he is able to fast.

**The twelfth issue:** Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "There is no ẓihār for women. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Those of you who make ẓihār from their wives﴾ and He did not say: ﴿The women among you who make ẓihār from their husbands﴾. Ẓihār is only for men." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is narrated from Ibn al-Qasim, Salim, Yahya ibn Sa'id, Rabi'ah and Abu al-Zinad. It is correct in meaning, because the authority to dissolve and to contract, and to make lawful and unlawful, in marriage lies in the hands of men; women have no share in it, and this is a consensus (ijma', the scholarly agreement)."

Abu 'Umar said: "There is no ẓihār for women according to the majority of scholars." Al-Hasan ibn Ziyad said: "It is a ẓihār (by the wife against the husband)." Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and Muhammad said: "A woman's ẓihār against a man is nothing, whether before the marriage or after it." Al-Shafi'i said: "There is no ẓihār from a woman toward a man." Al-Awza'i said: "If a woman says to her husband, 'You are to me like the back of my mother, So-and-so,' it is an oath, for which she makes expiation." Ishaq said likewise, and said: "A woman cannot be one who makes ẓihār against a man, but she must make an oath, for which she makes expiation." Al-Zuhri said: "I think she should make the expiation of ẓihār, and her saying this does not prevent her husband from having intercourse with her," narrated by Ma'mar from him. Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata', said: "She has made unlawful what Allah made lawful; for her is the expiation of an oath." This is the view of Abu Yusuf. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: "Nothing is incumbent upon her."

**The thirteenth issue:** Whoever has madness (lamam) and at some times his speech is coherent, if he makes ẓihār, his ẓihār is binding, because of what is reported in the ḥadīth that Khawlah bint Tha'labah, whose husband was Aws ibn al-Samit, and who had madness, was struck by some of his madness, and he made ẓihār against his wife.

**The fourteenth issue:** Whoever is angry and makes ẓihār against his wife, or divorces her, his anger does not remove the ruling from him. In some chains of this ḥadīth, Yusuf ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Salam said: "Khawlah, the wife of Aws ibn al-Samit, related to me, saying: 'There was something between me and him, and he said: "You are to me like the back of my mother," then he went out to the gathering of his people.' Her saying, 'There was something between me and him,' is evidence of a dispute that drove him (to it), so he made ẓihār against her." Anger is void: it does not lift a ruling nor change the law, and likewise the intoxicated person.

**The fifteenth issue:** The ruling of ẓihār and divorce applies to a man in the state of his intoxication if he understands his words and his speech is coherent, because of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿until you know what you are saying﴾, as its explanation was discussed earlier in (al-Nisa') (see vol. 5, p. 203). And Allah knows best.

**The sixteenth issue:** The one who makes ẓihār must not approach his wife, nor have intimate contact with her, nor take any pleasure from her in any way, until he makes expiation. This is contrary to one of al-Shafi'i's two opinions, because his saying, "You are to me like the back of my mother," requires the prohibition of every kind of enjoyment (of the wife), by its wording and its meaning. If he has intercourse with her before he makes expiation, he must seek forgiveness from Allah, the Exalted, and refrain from her until he makes one expiation. Mujahid and others said: "He must make two expiations."

Sa'id narrated from Qatadah, and Mutarrif from Raja' ibn Haywah, from Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb, from 'Amr ibn al-'As, concerning the one who makes ẓihār: if he has intercourse before he makes expiation, he must make two expiations. Ma'mar narrated from Qatadah, who said: "Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb said: He must make two expiations."

A group of the imams, among them Ibn Majah and al-Nasa'i, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that a man made ẓihār against his wife, then he had intercourse with her before he made expiation. He came to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned that to him. He said: "What drove you to that?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah! I saw the whiteness of her anklet in the light of the moon, and I could not control myself, and I fell upon her." The Prophet ﷺ laughed, and commanded him not to approach her until he made expiation.

Ibn Majah and al-Daraqutni narrated from Sulayman ibn Yasar, from Salamah ibn Sakhr, that he made ẓihār in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, then he had intercourse with his wife before he made expiation. He came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and that was mentioned to him, so he commanded him to make a single expiation.

**The eighteenth issue:** If a man makes ẓihār against four women in a single statement, such as his saying: "You are to me like the back of my mother," he is a ẓihār-maker against each one of them, and he is not permitted to have intercourse with any one of them, and one expiation suffices him. Al-Shafi'i said: "Four expiations are binding upon him." There is no evidence in the verse for any of that, because the plural form occurs only in the general address to the believers, and what is relied upon is the meaning. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: If a man has four wives under him and makes ẓihār against them, one expiation suffices him. If he makes ẓihār against one after another, then an expiation is binding upon him for each one of them." This is a consensus.

**The nineteenth issue:** If he says to four women: "If I marry you, then you are to me like the back of my mother," and then he marries one of them, he must not approach her until he makes expiation, and the oath is then dropped for the rest of them. It has been said: he must not have intercourse with the remaining ones until he makes expiation. The first view is the school's position.

**The twentieth issue:** If he says to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother, and you are divorced irrevocably (al-batta)," the divorce and the ẓihār are binding on him together. He does not make expiation until he marries her after another husband, and he must not have intercourse with her once he marries her until he makes expiation. [Note: by al-batta he means the triple divorce, as is understood from what follows and as in Ibn al-'Arabi, where he said: "If he divorced her three times after the ẓihār, then she returned to him by a new marriage, he must not have intercourse with her until he makes expiation."] If he says to her: "You are divorced irrevocably, and you are to me like the back of my mother," the divorce is binding on him but the ẓihār is not binding on him, because a woman who has been irrevocably divorced cannot be subject to another divorce.

**The twenty-first issue:** Some scholars said: the ẓihār of a woman who has not been consummated is not valid. Al-Muzani said: "ẓihār is not valid from a woman who has received a revocable divorce." This is nothing, because the rulings of marriage in both cases remain in force, and just as divorce applies to her, so too ẓihār applies to her, by analogy and by reasoning. And Allah knows best.

**The twenty-second issue:** His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿They are not their mothers﴾, that is, their wives are not their mothers. The common reading is (ummahatihim), with the ta' in the genitive, according to the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, as in His saying: (What is this, a human?) [ma hadha basharan]. Abu Ma'mar and al-Sulami and others read (ummahatuhum) with the nominative, according to the dialect of Tamim. Al-Farra' said: "The people of Najd and the tribe of Tamim say, 'ma hadha bashar,' and 'ma hunna ummahatuhum' with the nominative."

﴿Their mothers are none but those who bore them﴾, that is, their mothers are none but the women who gave birth to them. There is a proverb: "Your son is the one who bled your heels" (i.e., the one who was born from you). The discussion of (al-lla'i) was given earlier in (al-Ahzab). [Note: There is no discussion of al-lla'i in al-Ahzab, and it seems a gap occurred in the copies of the original that are in our hands.]

**The twenty-third issue:** His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed they utter a reprehensible word and a lie﴾, that is, a hideous word that is not known in the Sharia. Zur is falsehood. ﴿And indeed Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾, since He made the expiation for them a means of freeing them from this reprehensible saying.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 58, verses 3–4 (part 1 of 3):**

It contains twelve issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful (yuzahirun) from their wives﴾. This is a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾, with "upon them" (alayhim) omitted because the sense of the speech indicates it. That is, "upon them is the freeing of a neck." It was also said: that is, "their expiation is the freeing of a neck."

The matter agreed upon among the scholars concerning *zihar* (the pre-Islamic form of divorce-like oath, declaring one's wife unlawful) is a man saying to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother." This is the statement of falsehood and lie that Allah referred to with His saying: ﴿And indeed they say an objectionable word and a lie﴾. Whoever says this statement, his wife becomes unlawful for him to have intercourse with. Whoever returns to what he said is obligated to the expiation of *zihar*, because of the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful, then return to what they said, then the freeing of a neck﴾. This indicates that the expiation of *zihar* is not obligatory by the statement alone until the return (al-'awd) is joined to it. This is a difficult point over which people differed, with seven opinions.

The first: that it is the intention (al-'azm) to have intercourse. This is the well-known view of the Iraqis, Abu Hanifa and his companions. It is also reported from Malik: if he intends to have intercourse with her, it is a return; if he does not intend it, it is not a return.

The second: the intention to keep her after declaring *zihar* from her. This was said by Malik.

The third: the intention regarding both (intercourse and keeping her). This is Malik's view in his *Muwatta'*. Malik said, regarding the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful, then return to what they said﴾, he said: "I have heard that the explanation of that is that a man declares his wife unlawful, then he resolves to have intercourse with her and to keep her. If he resolves on that, the expiation becomes obligatory upon him. If he divorces her and, after declaring her unlawful, he does not resolve to keep her and have intercourse with her, then there is no expiation upon him." Malik said: "And if he marries her after that, he does not touch her until he has paid the expiation of *zihar*."

The fourth: that it is the intercourse itself. If he does not have intercourse, it is not a return. This was said by al-Hasan and also by Malik.

The fifth: Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is that he keeps her as a wife after the *zihar* while he is able to divorce her, because when he declared *zihar* he intended the prohibition. If he follows it with divorce, he has acted contrary to what he began by imposing the prohibition, and there is no expiation upon him. But if he refrains from divorce, he has returned to what he was upon, and so the expiation becomes obligatory upon him.

The sixth: that *zihar* makes unlawful a prohibition that only the expiation removes. According to those who hold this view, the meaning of "return" is that he may not make her lawful for intercourse except by an expiation that he pays first. This was said by Abu Hanifa and his companions, and by al-Layth ibn Sa'd.

The seventh: it is the repetition of *zihar* with its wording. This is the view of the Zahiris who reject analogy (qiyas). They said: if he repeats the wording of *zihar*, that is the return; and if he does not repeat it, it is not a return. This is attributed to Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj, Abu al-'Aliya, and also Abu Hanifa, and it is the view of al-Farra'. Abu al-'Aliya said: "The apparent meaning of the verse supports it, because He said: ﴿then return to what they said﴾, that is, to the statement of what they said."

Ali ibn Abi Talha reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful from their wives, then return to what they said﴾, that it is: he says to her, "You are to me like the back of my mother." When he says this to her, she is not lawful to him until he pays the expiation of *zihar*.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for the view that the return is a return to the wording of *zihar*, it is definitively false and not authentically transmitted from Bukayr. It is likely that it comes from the ignorance of Dawud and his followers. The narratives of those who declared *zihar* have been related, and in the mention of the expiation upon them there is no mention of a return of the statement from them. Furthermore, the meaning refutes it, because Allah described it as an objectionable word and a lie. How then can it be said to him: if you repeat the prohibited statement and the forbidden cause, the expiation becomes obligatory upon you? This is not rationally conceivable. Do you not see that every cause that makes expiation obligatory, such as killing or intercourse during fasting or other things, does not require repetition?

I (al-Qurtubi) say: This is a view that is likely to come from the ignorance of Dawud and his followers, and it has been borne upon it. Those we have mentioned who held Dawud's view said so. As for al-Shafi'i's view, that he left divorce while able to do it, it is refuted by three fundamental points:

The first: He said "then" (thumma), and its outward meaning requires delay.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, "then they return" requires the existence of an action from them, and the passage of time is not an action from them.

The third: A revocable divorce does not contradict remaining in the marital bond, so the ruling of *zihar* has not lapsed, just as with *ila'* (the oath of abstention from intercourse).

If it is said: If he sees her as his mother, he does not keep her, since keeping a mother in marriage is not valid. This is the main argument of the people of Transoxiana. We say: If he resolves to act contrary to what he said, and sees her as other than his mother, he makes expiation and returns to his wife.

The verification of this view is that the resolve is an inner statement. This man said a statement that entailed permissibility, which is marriage, and said a statement that entailed prohibition, which is *zihar*. Then he returned to what he had said, which is permissibility. It is not valid that it be a new contract from him, because the contract still stands. So nothing remains except that it is an inner statement of resolve that contradicts what he believed and said to himself about the *zihar* that he reported with his words, "You are to me like the back of my mother." When that is the case, he makes expiation and returns to his family, because of His saying: ﴿before they touch one another﴾. This is an excellent explanation [in its field] [[The addition is from Ahkam al-Quran of Ibn al-'Arabi.]].

**The second issue:** Some of the interpreters of the Qur'an said: the verse contains an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir). The meaning is: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful, then return﴾ to what they were upon of intercourse, ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾ for what they said. That is, upon them is the freeing of a neck because of what they said. So the preposition in His saying, ﴿for what they said﴾, is related to the omitted element that is the predicate of the subject, which is "upon them." This was said by al-Akhfash.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "then they return to the desire for intercourse because of what they said."

It was also said: the meaning is those who used to declare *zihar* from their wives in the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period), then return, in Islam, to what they had said in the Jahiliyya; so the expiation for whoever returns is that he frees a neck.

Al-Farra' said: the *lam* (in "li-ma") is in the sense of "'an" (from), and the meaning is "then they retract what they said and intend intercourse."

Al-Akhfash said: "for what they said" and "to what they said" are one and the same, and *lam* and *ila* (to) are interchangeable. He cited: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who guided us to this﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 208]], and: ﴿so guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 83]], and: ﴿because your Lord has inspired to her﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 149]], and: ﴿And it was revealed to Noah﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 29]].

**The third issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾, that is, upon him is the emancipation of a neck. It is said: *harrartuhu*, meaning I made him free. Then this neck must be complete and sound, free of every defect. Among its completeness, according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, is that it be Muslim, like the neck in the expiation for killing. According to Abu Hanifa and his companions, a disbeliever is acceptable, and so is one who has some trace of servitude, such as a *mukatab* (a slave under a contract of self-purchase) and others. [In manuscripts H, Z, S, T, L: "a share of slavery," and the meaning is the same.]

**The fourth issue:** If he frees half of two slaves, it is not sufficient according to us, nor according to Abu Hanifa. Al-Shafi'i said it is sufficient, because half of two slaves is in the sense of one slave, and because the expiation by emancipation is by way of property, so it is permissible for it to admit partition and division, like feeding the poor. Our evidence is His saying: ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾, and this term refers to one individual person, and part of a neck is not a neck. Such a matter does not admit of patching together, because the act of worship connected to a neck is not fulfilled by half of two necks, the root of which is when two men share in two sacrificial animals. Also, if he commissions two men to perform one pilgrimage on his behalf, it is not permissible for either of them to perform half of it for him, likewise here. Also, if he bequeaths that a neck be bought and freed on his behalf, it is not permissible to free half of two slaves on his behalf; likewise in our case. By this, their evidence is invalidated. Feeding and other things are not divisible in expiation according to us.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿before they touch one another﴾, meaning before he has intercourse with her. It is not permissible for the one who has made zihar (the pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband likens his wife to his mother's back) to have intercourse with her before the expiation (kaffarah). If he has intercourse with her before the expiation, he has sinned and disobeyed, and the expiation does not fall away from him.

It is reported from Mujahid that if he has intercourse before he begins the expiation, he is obliged to pay another expiation. It is also reported from others that the expiation required by zihar falls away from him and nothing at all is obligatory on him, because Allah, exalted is He, required the expiation and commanded it before touching, so if he delayed it until he touched her, its time has passed.

The sound view is that the expiation remains obligatory, because by his intercourse he has committed a sin, and this does not cancel the expiation. He performs it as a make-up (qada'), just as if he had delayed the prayer beyond its time. In the hadith of Aws ibn al-Samit, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was informed that he had had intercourse with his wife, he commanded him to perform the expiation.[[The return (al-'awd) is not mentioned earlier in the hadith of Aws; rather, it concerns another person who made zihar, and he is the one who said: "I saw her anklet in the light of the moon."]] This is an explicit text. It applies whether the expiation is by freeing a slave, by fasting, or by feeding the poor.

Abu Hanifa said: if his expiation is by feeding the poor, it is permissible for him to have intercourse and then feed the poor.

As for other than intercourse, such as kissing, bodily contact, and sensual enjoyment, these are not prohibited according to the majority of scholars. This is the view of al-Hasan and Sufyan, and it is the sound position in the school of al-Shafi'i. It has also been said that all of these are prohibited, and that all the meanings of touching (al-masis) are included. This is the view of Malik and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i.

This has already been discussed.

**The sixth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is what you are admonished with﴾, meaning you are commanded with it. ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, meaning of the expiation and other matters.

**The seventh issue:** Whoever cannot find a slave (raqaba) or the price of one, or who owns one but is in great need of her for his service, or who owns the price of one but needs it for his own maintenance, or who has a dwelling that is his only one and has nothing else, then he may fast according to al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said: he does not fast, and the obligation of freeing a slave remains upon him even if he is in need of that. Malik said: if he has a house and a servant, the obligation of freeing a slave falls upon him, and if he is unable to free a slave, then:

**The eighth issue:** He must fast two consecutive months. If he breaks the fast in the course of them without an excuse, he begins them again. If he breaks it for an excuse, such as travel or illness, it has been said that he continues (yabni), as stated by Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, 'Umar ibn Dinar, and al-Sha'bi. This is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i and is the sound position in his school. Malik said: if he falls ill during the fasting of the expiation of zihar, he continues from where he left off once he recovers. The position of Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) is that he begins anew. This is also one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i.

**The ninth issue:** If he began the fast and then found a slave, he completes the fast and it is valid according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, because he was commanded with that when he entered into it. According to Abu Hanifa and his companions, he breaks the fast and frees a slave, by analogy with a young girl in a waiting period counted in months who sees blood before its completion, for she begins the menstrual period anew, by consensus of the scholars. If he set out on a journey during his fast and broke it, he begins the fast anew according to Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Abu Hanifa, because of His saying: (consecutive). According to the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, he continues, because it is an excuse, and by analogy with Ramadan. If there intervenes a period in which fasting for the expiation is not permitted, such as the two festivals and the month of Ramadan, the consecutiveness is broken.

**The tenth issue:** If the one who made zihar has intercourse during the two months, by day, the consecutiveness is broken according to al-Shafi'i; by night, it is not broken, because night is not a time for fasting. Malik and Abu Hanifa said: it is broken in every case, and he is obliged to begin the expiation anew, because of His saying: ﴿before they touch one another﴾. This condition applies to the whole of the two months and to parts of them. So if he has intercourse before they are completed, that is not the fasting that was commanded, and he is obliged to begin it anew, just as if he said: "Pray before you speak to Zayd," and then he spoke to Zayd during the prayer; or if he said: "Pray before you see Zayd," and he saw him during the prayer, he is obliged to begin the prayer anew, because this prayer is not the one that was commanded. Likewise here. And Allah knows best.

**The eleventh issue:** Whoever has an illness that lasts so long that recovery is not expected is in the position of one who is incapable due to old age, and it is permissible for him to switch from fasting to feeding the poor. If his illness is one from which recovery is expected, and his need to have intercourse with his wife is very intense, it is preferable for him to wait for recovery until he is able to fast. If he expiates by feeding the poor without waiting for the ability to fast, it is valid.

**The twelfth issue:** Whoever makes zihar while poor and then becomes wealthy, fasting does not suffice for him. Whoever makes zihar while wealthy and then becomes poor before expiating, fasts. The consideration is only his condition on the day he expiates. If he had intercourse with her while he was without means and in hardship, and did not fast until he became wealthy, he is obliged to free a slave. If he began fasting and then became wealthy, then if a reasonable portion of his fast had passed, about a week or similar, he continues. If it was only a day or two or similar, he abandons the fast and returns to freeing a slave, and that is not obligatory on him. Do you not see that it is not obligatory upon one for whom water becomes available, who has already entered the prayer after performing tayammum (dry ablution), to break off and begin the purification anew, according to Malik?

**The thirteenth issue:** If he frees two slaves for two expiations, whether of zihar, of homicide, or for breaking the fast in Ramadan, and he shares between them so that each is counted for both, it does not suffice for him. This is equivalent to one who frees one slave for two expiations. Likewise, if he fasts for four months for both, so as to fast two months for each of them, it does not suffice. It has been said that it suffices. If he makes zihar with respect to two women, and frees a slave for one of them without specifying which, he may not have intercourse with either of them until he performs another expiation. If he specifies the expiation for one of them, he may have intercourse with her before he performs the expiation for the other. If he makes zihar with respect to four women and frees three slaves on their behalf and fasts two months, neither the freeing nor the fasting suffices for him, because he has fasted for each of them only fifteen days. If he expiates on their behalf by feeding the poor, it is permissible for him to feed two hundred poor people on their behalf. If he cannot do so, he may distribute it in portions. This differs from freeing and fasting, because fasting two months cannot be divided, whereas feeding can be divided.

**Section.** It contains six issues.

**The first issue:** Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned the expiation here in graded order. There is no way to fasting except when one is unable to free a slave, and likewise there is no way to feeding the poor except when one is unable to fast. Whoever is unable to fast is obliged to feed sixty poor persons, two mudd for each poor person, the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ). If he feeds one mudd by the mudd of Hisham, which is two mudd less a third, or he feeds one and a half mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), it suffices for him. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: the best of this is two mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), because Allah, mighty and majestic, did not say in the expiation of zihar: ﴿from the average of what you feed your families﴾,[[See vol. 6, p. 265.]] so it is obligatory to aim at satiety. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Malik said, in the narration of Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam: one mudd by the mudd of Hisham, and that is satiety here, because Allah, exalted is He, left the food unrestricted and did not mention the average. In the narration of Ashhab he said: two mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said to him: "Did you not say one mudd by the mudd of Hisham?" He said: "Yes, but two mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ) is more beloved to me." And Ibn al-Qasim also reported the same from him.

I say: this is the transmission of Ibn Wahb and Mutarrif from Malik, that he gives two mudds to each needy person by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is also the position of Abu Hanifa and his companions. The position of al-Shafi'i and others is one mudd for each needy person, and he is not obliged to give more than that, because he is making expiation by feeding and was not required to give more than a mudd, and its origin is the expiation for breaking the fast and for oaths. Our evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then feeding sixty needy people﴾. The unrestricted term "feeding" includes satiety, and by custom that is not achieved with one mudd except with something added to it. Likewise Ashhab said: I said to Malik, "Does satiety differ between us and you?" He said, "Yes! Satiety for us is a mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), and satiety for you is greater, because the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed for blessing for us and not for you, so you eat more than we eat." Abu al-Hasan al-Qabisi said: The people of Medina only adopted the mudd of Hisham in the expiation of zihar (the pre-Islamic divorce formula of likening a wife to one's mother) as a severity against those who make zihar, concerning whom God bore witness that they speak an objectionable word and a falsehood. Ibn al-'Arabi said: The discussion has arisen here about the mudd of Hisham, as you see, and I wish that time would shatter its mention and erase its trace from the books, for the city in which revelation descended, in which the Messenger settled, and in which zihar occurred, and to which it was said: ﴿then feeding sixty needy people﴾, they understood it and knew what was meant by it, that it is satiety, and its measure was known to them and fixed in their minds. That satiety is mentioned in the reports many times, and the situation remained so during the days of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, until Satan blew into the ear of Hisham, and he saw that the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ) did not satisfy him, nor those like him among his entourage and peers, so he made it seem good to him to adopt a mudd in which his satiety would be, so he made it two ratls and compelled the people to it, and when it became wet it returned to about three ratls, thus he changed the Sunnah and removed the place of blessing. The Prophet (ﷺ), when he prayed to his Lord for the people of Medina that blessing would remain for them in their mudd and their sa', like what He blessed for Abraham in Mecca, the blessing kept flowing by the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his mudd. Then Satan strove to change this Sunnah and remove this blessing, and none responded to him in that except Hisham. It was the duty of the scholars to abandon [[In L: "yad'u" instead of "yalghu".]] its mention and erase its trace, if they did not change its rule. As for referring to its mention in rulings and making it an explanation of what God and His Messenger mentioned, after it had been clear to the Companions among whom it was revealed, that is a grave matter. For this reason, the transmission of Ashhab, which mentions two mudds by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the expiation of zihar, is more beloved to us than the report that it is by the mudd of Hisham. Do you not see how Malik drew attention to this knowledge by his saying to Ashhab: "Satiety for us is by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), and satiety for you is greater, because the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed for us for blessing." I say this too, for when worship is performed according to the Sunnah, if it is bodily it is quicker to be accepted, and if it is financial its little is heavier in the scale, more blessed in the hand of the taker, sweeter in his mouth, less harmful in his belly, and more upholding of his backbone [[In H, Z, S, H: "for his heart."]]. And God knows best [[In H, Z, S, L, H: "and God is the Granter of success, there is no lord but Him."]].

The second issue: according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, it is not valid to feed fewer than sixty needy people. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: if he feeds one needy person each day half a sa' until he completes the number, it suffices for him.

The third issue: Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: It is a strange matter that Abu Hanifa said that the restriction of a free person is void, and he argued with His saying, exalted is He: (then the freeing of a neck), and did not distinguish between the mature and the wastrel. This is weak jurisprudence unbefitting his rank, for this verse is general, and the judgment of restraint was widespread among the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and reason requires it. Whoever is under restraint due to minority or guardianship, and then becomes a wastrel, has been forbidden to hand over property to him, so how could his action be enforced concerning it when the specific governs the general?

The fourth issue: according to some scholars, the ruling on zihar abrogates the practice they had of considering zihar to be a divorce, and this meaning has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Qilaba and others.

The fifth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is so that you may believe in God and His Messenger﴾, meaning: that which We have described of severity in the expiation. (So that you may believe) means: so that you may affirm that God commanded it. Some scholars have used this to argue that this expiation is faith in God, exalted and glorified is He, because He mentioned it and made it obligatory, and said: (That is so that you may believe in God and His Messenger), meaning: that is so that you may be obedient to God, exalted is He, standing at His limits and not transgressing them. So He named the expiation faith because it is obedience and observance of the limit. Thus it is established that everything resembling it is faith. If it is said: the meaning of His saying, "That is so that you may believe in God and His Messenger," is: so that you do not return to zihar, which is an objectionable word and falsehood.
It is said to him: it may be that this is intended and the first is intended too, so the meaning is: that is so that you do not return to the objectionable word and falsehood, but rather you abandon both as obedience to God, exalted is He, since He has forbidden them; and so that you avoid the one who makes zihar with her until you make expiation, since God forbade touching her; and so that you make expiation, since God, exalted is He, commanded the expiation and required its payment from you. Thus by all this you will be believers in God and His Messenger, for these are limits you guard and acts of obedience you perform, and obedience to God and to His Messenger (ﷺ) is faith. And success is from God.

The sixth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And these are the limits of God﴾, meaning: He made clear His disobedience and His obedience. So His disobedience is zihar, and His obedience is the expiation.
(And for the disbelievers there is a painful punishment), meaning: for whoever does not affirm the rulings of God, exalted is He, is the punishment of Hell.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 58, verses 3–4 (part 1 of 3):**

It contains twelve issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful (yuzahirun) from their wives﴾. This is a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾, with "upon them" (alayhim) omitted because the sense of the speech indicates it. That is, "upon them is the freeing of a neck." It was also said: that is, "their expiation is the freeing of a neck."

The matter agreed upon among the scholars concerning *zihar* (the pre-Islamic form of divorce-like oath, declaring one's wife unlawful) is a man saying to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother." This is the statement of falsehood and lie that Allah referred to with His saying: ﴿And indeed they say an objectionable word and a lie﴾. Whoever says this statement, his wife becomes unlawful for him to have intercourse with. Whoever returns to what he said is obligated to the expiation of *zihar*, because of the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful, then return to what they said, then the freeing of a neck﴾. This indicates that the expiation of *zihar* is not obligatory by the statement alone until the return (al-'awd) is joined to it. This is a difficult point over which people differed, with seven opinions.

The first: that it is the intention (al-'azm) to have intercourse. This is the well-known view of the Iraqis, Abu Hanifa and his companions. It is also reported from Malik: if he intends to have intercourse with her, it is a return; if he does not intend it, it is not a return.

The second: the intention to keep her after declaring *zihar* from her. This was said by Malik.

The third: the intention regarding both (intercourse and keeping her). This is Malik's view in his *Muwatta'*. Malik said, regarding the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful, then return to what they said﴾, he said: "I have heard that the explanation of that is that a man declares his wife unlawful, then he resolves to have intercourse with her and to keep her. If he resolves on that, the expiation becomes obligatory upon him. If he divorces her and, after declaring her unlawful, he does not resolve to keep her and have intercourse with her, then there is no expiation upon him." Malik said: "And if he marries her after that, he does not touch her until he has paid the expiation of *zihar*."

The fourth: that it is the intercourse itself. If he does not have intercourse, it is not a return. This was said by al-Hasan and also by Malik.

The fifth: Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is that he keeps her as a wife after the *zihar* while he is able to divorce her, because when he declared *zihar* he intended the prohibition. If he follows it with divorce, he has acted contrary to what he began by imposing the prohibition, and there is no expiation upon him. But if he refrains from divorce, he has returned to what he was upon, and so the expiation becomes obligatory upon him.

The sixth: that *zihar* makes unlawful a prohibition that only the expiation removes. According to those who hold this view, the meaning of "return" is that he may not make her lawful for intercourse except by an expiation that he pays first. This was said by Abu Hanifa and his companions, and by al-Layth ibn Sa'd.

The seventh: it is the repetition of *zihar* with its wording. This is the view of the Zahiris who reject analogy (qiyas). They said: if he repeats the wording of *zihar*, that is the return; and if he does not repeat it, it is not a return. This is attributed to Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj, Abu al-'Aliya, and also Abu Hanifa, and it is the view of al-Farra'. Abu al-'Aliya said: "The apparent meaning of the verse supports it, because He said: ﴿then return to what they said﴾, that is, to the statement of what they said."

Ali ibn Abi Talha reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful from their wives, then return to what they said﴾, that it is: he says to her, "You are to me like the back of my mother." When he says this to her, she is not lawful to him until he pays the expiation of *zihar*.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for the view that the return is a return to the wording of *zihar*, it is definitively false and not authentically transmitted from Bukayr. It is likely that it comes from the ignorance of Dawud and his followers. The narratives of those who declared *zihar* have been related, and in the mention of the expiation upon them there is no mention of a return of the statement from them. Furthermore, the meaning refutes it, because Allah described it as an objectionable word and a lie. How then can it be said to him: if you repeat the prohibited statement and the forbidden cause, the expiation becomes obligatory upon you? This is not rationally conceivable. Do you not see that every cause that makes expiation obligatory, such as killing or intercourse during fasting or other things, does not require repetition?

I (al-Qurtubi) say: This is a view that is likely to come from the ignorance of Dawud and his followers, and it has been borne upon it. Those we have mentioned who held Dawud's view said so. As for al-Shafi'i's view, that he left divorce while able to do it, it is refuted by three fundamental points:

The first: He said "then" (thumma), and its outward meaning requires delay.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, "then they return" requires the existence of an action from them, and the passage of time is not an action from them.

The third: A revocable divorce does not contradict remaining in the marital bond, so the ruling of *zihar* has not lapsed, just as with *ila'* (the oath of abstention from intercourse).

If it is said: If he sees her as his mother, he does not keep her, since keeping a mother in marriage is not valid. This is the main argument of the people of Transoxiana. We say: If he resolves to act contrary to what he said, and sees her as other than his mother, he makes expiation and returns to his wife.

The verification of this view is that the resolve is an inner statement. This man said a statement that entailed permissibility, which is marriage, and said a statement that entailed prohibition, which is *zihar*. Then he returned to what he had said, which is permissibility. It is not valid that it be a new contract from him, because the contract still stands. So nothing remains except that it is an inner statement of resolve that contradicts what he believed and said to himself about the *zihar* that he reported with his words, "You are to me like the back of my mother." When that is the case, he makes expiation and returns to his family, because of His saying: ﴿before they touch one another﴾. This is an excellent explanation [in its field] [[The addition is from Ahkam al-Quran of Ibn al-'Arabi.]].

**The second issue:** Some of the interpreters of the Qur'an said: the verse contains an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir). The meaning is: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful, then return﴾ to what they were upon of intercourse, ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾ for what they said. That is, upon them is the freeing of a neck because of what they said. So the preposition in His saying, ﴿for what they said﴾, is related to the omitted element that is the predicate of the subject, which is "upon them." This was said by al-Akhfash.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "then they return to the desire for intercourse because of what they said."

It was also said: the meaning is those who used to declare *zihar* from their wives in the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period), then return, in Islam, to what they had said in the Jahiliyya; so the expiation for whoever returns is that he frees a neck.

Al-Farra' said: the *lam* (in "li-ma") is in the sense of "'an" (from), and the meaning is "then they retract what they said and intend intercourse."

Al-Akhfash said: "for what they said" and "to what they said" are one and the same, and *lam* and *ila* (to) are interchangeable. He cited: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who guided us to this﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 208]], and: ﴿so guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 83]], and: ﴿because your Lord has inspired to her﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 149]], and: ﴿And it was revealed to Noah﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 29]].

**The third issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾, that is, upon him is the emancipation of a neck. It is said: *harrartuhu*, meaning I made him free. Then this neck must be complete and sound, free of every defect. Among its completeness, according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, is that it be Muslim, like the neck in the expiation for killing. According to Abu Hanifa and his companions, a disbeliever is acceptable, and so is one who has some trace of servitude, such as a *mukatab* (a slave under a contract of self-purchase) and others. [In manuscripts H, Z, S, T, L: "a share of slavery," and the meaning is the same.]

**The fourth issue:** If he frees half of two slaves, it is not sufficient according to us, nor according to Abu Hanifa. Al-Shafi'i said it is sufficient, because half of two slaves is in the sense of one slave, and because the expiation by emancipation is by way of property, so it is permissible for it to admit partition and division, like feeding the poor. Our evidence is His saying: ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾, and this term refers to one individual person, and part of a neck is not a neck. Such a matter does not admit of patching together, because the act of worship connected to a neck is not fulfilled by half of two necks, the root of which is when two men share in two sacrificial animals. Also, if he commissions two men to perform one pilgrimage on his behalf, it is not permissible for either of them to perform half of it for him, likewise here. Also, if he bequeaths that a neck be bought and freed on his behalf, it is not permissible to free half of two slaves on his behalf; likewise in our case. By this, their evidence is invalidated. Feeding and other things are not divisible in expiation according to us.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿before they touch one another﴾, meaning before he has intercourse with her. It is not permissible for the one who has made zihar (the pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband likens his wife to his mother's back) to have intercourse with her before the expiation (kaffarah). If he has intercourse with her before the expiation, he has sinned and disobeyed, and the expiation does not fall away from him.

It is reported from Mujahid that if he has intercourse before he begins the expiation, he is obliged to pay another expiation. It is also reported from others that the expiation required by zihar falls away from him and nothing at all is obligatory on him, because Allah, exalted is He, required the expiation and commanded it before touching, so if he delayed it until he touched her, its time has passed.

The sound view is that the expiation remains obligatory, because by his intercourse he has committed a sin, and this does not cancel the expiation. He performs it as a make-up (qada'), just as if he had delayed the prayer beyond its time. In the hadith of Aws ibn al-Samit, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was informed that he had had intercourse with his wife, he commanded him to perform the expiation.[[The return (al-'awd) is not mentioned earlier in the hadith of Aws; rather, it concerns another person who made zihar, and he is the one who said: "I saw her anklet in the light of the moon."]] This is an explicit text. It applies whether the expiation is by freeing a slave, by fasting, or by feeding the poor.

Abu Hanifa said: if his expiation is by feeding the poor, it is permissible for him to have intercourse and then feed the poor.

As for other than intercourse, such as kissing, bodily contact, and sensual enjoyment, these are not prohibited according to the majority of scholars. This is the view of al-Hasan and Sufyan, and it is the sound position in the school of al-Shafi'i. It has also been said that all of these are prohibited, and that all the meanings of touching (al-masis) are included. This is the view of Malik and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i.

This has already been discussed.

**The sixth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is what you are admonished with﴾, meaning you are commanded with it. ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, meaning of the expiation and other matters.

**The seventh issue:** Whoever cannot find a slave (raqaba) or the price of one, or who owns one but is in great need of her for his service, or who owns the price of one but needs it for his own maintenance, or who has a dwelling that is his only one and has nothing else, then he may fast according to al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said: he does not fast, and the obligation of freeing a slave remains upon him even if he is in need of that. Malik said: if he has a house and a servant, the obligation of freeing a slave falls upon him, and if he is unable to free a slave, then:

**The eighth issue:** He must fast two consecutive months. If he breaks the fast in the course of them without an excuse, he begins them again. If he breaks it for an excuse, such as travel or illness, it has been said that he continues (yabni), as stated by Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, 'Umar ibn Dinar, and al-Sha'bi. This is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i and is the sound position in his school. Malik said: if he falls ill during the fasting of the expiation of zihar, he continues from where he left off once he recovers. The position of Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) is that he begins anew. This is also one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i.

**The ninth issue:** If he began the fast and then found a slave, he completes the fast and it is valid according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, because he was commanded with that when he entered into it. According to Abu Hanifa and his companions, he breaks the fast and frees a slave, by analogy with a young girl in a waiting period counted in months who sees blood before its completion, for she begins the menstrual period anew, by consensus of the scholars. If he set out on a journey during his fast and broke it, he begins the fast anew according to Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Abu Hanifa, because of His saying: (consecutive). According to the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, he continues, because it is an excuse, and by analogy with Ramadan. If there intervenes a period in which fasting for the expiation is not permitted, such as the two festivals and the month of Ramadan, the consecutiveness is broken.

**The tenth issue:** If the one who made zihar has intercourse during the two months, by day, the consecutiveness is broken according to al-Shafi'i; by night, it is not broken, because night is not a time for fasting. Malik and Abu Hanifa said: it is broken in every case, and he is obliged to begin the expiation anew, because of His saying: ﴿before they touch one another﴾. This condition applies to the whole of the two months and to parts of them. So if he has intercourse before they are completed, that is not the fasting that was commanded, and he is obliged to begin it anew, just as if he said: "Pray before you speak to Zayd," and then he spoke to Zayd during the prayer; or if he said: "Pray before you see Zayd," and he saw him during the prayer, he is obliged to begin the prayer anew, because this prayer is not the one that was commanded. Likewise here. And Allah knows best.

**The eleventh issue:** Whoever has an illness that lasts so long that recovery is not expected is in the position of one who is incapable due to old age, and it is permissible for him to switch from fasting to feeding the poor. If his illness is one from which recovery is expected, and his need to have intercourse with his wife is very intense, it is preferable for him to wait for recovery until he is able to fast. If he expiates by feeding the poor without waiting for the ability to fast, it is valid.

**The twelfth issue:** Whoever makes zihar while poor and then becomes wealthy, fasting does not suffice for him. Whoever makes zihar while wealthy and then becomes poor before expiating, fasts. The consideration is only his condition on the day he expiates. If he had intercourse with her while he was without means and in hardship, and did not fast until he became wealthy, he is obliged to free a slave. If he began fasting and then became wealthy, then if a reasonable portion of his fast had passed, about a week or similar, he continues. If it was only a day or two or similar, he abandons the fast and returns to freeing a slave, and that is not obligatory on him. Do you not see that it is not obligatory upon one for whom water becomes available, who has already entered the prayer after performing tayammum (dry ablution), to break off and begin the purification anew, according to Malik?

**The thirteenth issue:** If he frees two slaves for two expiations, whether of zihar, of homicide, or for breaking the fast in Ramadan, and he shares between them so that each is counted for both, it does not suffice for him. This is equivalent to one who frees one slave for two expiations. Likewise, if he fasts for four months for both, so as to fast two months for each of them, it does not suffice. It has been said that it suffices. If he makes zihar with respect to two women, and frees a slave for one of them without specifying which, he may not have intercourse with either of them until he performs another expiation. If he specifies the expiation for one of them, he may have intercourse with her before he performs the expiation for the other. If he makes zihar with respect to four women and frees three slaves on their behalf and fasts two months, neither the freeing nor the fasting suffices for him, because he has fasted for each of them only fifteen days. If he expiates on their behalf by feeding the poor, it is permissible for him to feed two hundred poor people on their behalf. If he cannot do so, he may distribute it in portions. This differs from freeing and fasting, because fasting two months cannot be divided, whereas feeding can be divided.

**Section.** It contains six issues.

**The first issue:** Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned the expiation here in graded order. There is no way to fasting except when one is unable to free a slave, and likewise there is no way to feeding the poor except when one is unable to fast. Whoever is unable to fast is obliged to feed sixty poor persons, two mudd for each poor person, the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ). If he feeds one mudd by the mudd of Hisham, which is two mudd less a third, or he feeds one and a half mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), it suffices for him. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: the best of this is two mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), because Allah, mighty and majestic, did not say in the expiation of zihar: ﴿from the average of what you feed your families﴾,[[See vol. 6, p. 265.]] so it is obligatory to aim at satiety. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Malik said, in the narration of Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam: one mudd by the mudd of Hisham, and that is satiety here, because Allah, exalted is He, left the food unrestricted and did not mention the average. In the narration of Ashhab he said: two mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said to him: "Did you not say one mudd by the mudd of Hisham?" He said: "Yes, but two mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ) is more beloved to me." And Ibn al-Qasim also reported the same from him.

I say: this is the transmission of Ibn Wahb and Mutarrif from Malik, that he gives two mudds to each needy person by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is also the position of Abu Hanifa and his companions. The position of al-Shafi'i and others is one mudd for each needy person, and he is not obliged to give more than that, because he is making expiation by feeding and was not required to give more than a mudd, and its origin is the expiation for breaking the fast and for oaths. Our evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then feeding sixty needy people﴾. The unrestricted term "feeding" includes satiety, and by custom that is not achieved with one mudd except with something added to it. Likewise Ashhab said: I said to Malik, "Does satiety differ between us and you?" He said, "Yes! Satiety for us is a mudd by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), and satiety for you is greater, because the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed for blessing for us and not for you, so you eat more than we eat." Abu al-Hasan al-Qabisi said: The people of Medina only adopted the mudd of Hisham in the expiation of zihar (the pre-Islamic divorce formula of likening a wife to one's mother) as a severity against those who make zihar, concerning whom God bore witness that they speak an objectionable word and a falsehood. Ibn al-'Arabi said: The discussion has arisen here about the mudd of Hisham, as you see, and I wish that time would shatter its mention and erase its trace from the books, for the city in which revelation descended, in which the Messenger settled, and in which zihar occurred, and to which it was said: ﴿then feeding sixty needy people﴾, they understood it and knew what was meant by it, that it is satiety, and its measure was known to them and fixed in their minds. That satiety is mentioned in the reports many times, and the situation remained so during the days of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, until Satan blew into the ear of Hisham, and he saw that the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ) did not satisfy him, nor those like him among his entourage and peers, so he made it seem good to him to adopt a mudd in which his satiety would be, so he made it two ratls and compelled the people to it, and when it became wet it returned to about three ratls, thus he changed the Sunnah and removed the place of blessing. The Prophet (ﷺ), when he prayed to his Lord for the people of Medina that blessing would remain for them in their mudd and their sa', like what He blessed for Abraham in Mecca, the blessing kept flowing by the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his mudd. Then Satan strove to change this Sunnah and remove this blessing, and none responded to him in that except Hisham. It was the duty of the scholars to abandon [[In L: "yad'u" instead of "yalghu".]] its mention and erase its trace, if they did not change its rule. As for referring to its mention in rulings and making it an explanation of what God and His Messenger mentioned, after it had been clear to the Companions among whom it was revealed, that is a grave matter. For this reason, the transmission of Ashhab, which mentions two mudds by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the expiation of zihar, is more beloved to us than the report that it is by the mudd of Hisham. Do you not see how Malik drew attention to this knowledge by his saying to Ashhab: "Satiety for us is by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), and satiety for you is greater, because the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed for us for blessing." I say this too, for when worship is performed according to the Sunnah, if it is bodily it is quicker to be accepted, and if it is financial its little is heavier in the scale, more blessed in the hand of the taker, sweeter in his mouth, less harmful in his belly, and more upholding of his backbone [[In H, Z, S, H: "for his heart."]]. And God knows best [[In H, Z, S, L, H: "and God is the Granter of success, there is no lord but Him."]].
